Original heading

Hezekiah destroys idolatry.

Hezekiah's reforms continue

After celebrating the Passover, the Israelites worked energetically to destroy the monuments of idolatry.

Public worship should encourage us to cleanse our hearts, homes and workplaces from the pollution of sin and the idolatry of greed.

It should also move us to encourage others to do the same.

How we respond after a solemn act of worship is extremely important for our personal faith, our families and public religion.

The people had tasted the sweetness of the recent Passover and therefore contributed willingly to support temple worship.

Those who genuinely enjoy the benefits of a steady and faithful ministry will not resent the expense of supporting it.

Hezekiah was wholehearted in his purpose and sincere in his dependence upon God in everything he did for the Lord.

God granted him success.

Whether we have many gifts or few, may we work to use and develop them and encourage others to do likewise.

Work undertaken sincerely for God's glory will finally bring us honor and comfort.
classic_reading:
[2Chr.31.1]
Chapter 31
Hezekiah destroys idolatry.
--After the passover, the people of Israel applied with vigour to destroy the monuments of idolatry. Public ordinances should stir us up to cleanse our hearts, our houses, and shops, from the filth of sin, and the idolatry of covetousness, and to excite others to do the same. The after-improvement of solemn ordinances, is of the greatest importance to personal, family, and public religion. When they had tasted the sweetness of God's ordinance in the late passover, they were free in maintaining the temple service. Those who enjoy the benefit of a settled ministry, will not grudge the expense of it. In all that Hezekiah attempted in God's service, he was earnest and single in his aim and dependence, and was prospered accordingly. Whether we have few or many talents intrusted to us, may we thus seek to improve them, and encourage others to do the same. What is undertaken with a sincere regard to the glory of God, will succeed to our own honour and comfort at last.

Sennacherib invades Judah (verses 1–23)

Those who trust God to keep them safe must still use appropriate means of protection; otherwise they are testing him.

God will provide, but we must also take responsible action.

Hezekiah gathered his people and spoke words of comfort to them.

Confidence in the Lord raises believers above the fear of human beings.

Let faithful subjects and soldiers of Jesus Christ rest upon his word and boldly declare, “If God is for us, who can be against us?”

Through God's favor, enemies are defeated and friends are gained.

Hezekiah's illness and death (verses 24–33)

God allowed Hezekiah to experience a trial without the usual supporting grace.

This exposed what remained in his heart and showed that he was not as mature in grace as he imagined.

It is good to discover our own weakness and sinfulness so that we do not become conceited or self-confident.

We must live in continual dependence on divine grace.

We do not know how corrupt our hearts may become or what we might do if God leaves us to ourselves.

Hezekiah's sin was that his heart became proud.

People who are great, godly or useful need especially to examine their weaknesses and remember how much they owe to freely given grace.

Let us ask God earnestly to keep us humble.

Hezekiah repaid the Lord poorly by turning the very gifts he had received into fuel for his pride.

We should avoid occasions of sin: company, amusements, books and even sights that feed our sinful desires.

Let us continually commit ourselves to the Lord's care and ask him never to abandon us.

Blessed be God, death will finally end the believer's conflict.

Then pride and every other sin will be abolished.

Never again will a believer be tempted to withhold the praise that belongs to the God of salvation.

Verses 1-23
Those who trust God with their safety, must use proper means, else they tempt him. God will provide, but so must we also. Hezekiah gathered his people together, and spake comfortably to them. A believing confidence in God, will raise us above the prevailing fear of man. Let the good subjects and soldiers of Jesus Christ, rest upon his word, and boldly say, Since God is for us, who can be against us? By the favour of God, enemies are lost, and friends gained.
[2Chr.32.24-2Chr.32.33]
Verses 24-33
God left Hezekiah to himself, that, by this trial and his weakness in it, what was in his heart might be known; that he was not so perfect in grace as he thought he was. It is good for us to know ourselves, and our own weakness and sinfulness, that we may not be conceited, or self-confident, but may always live in dependence upon Divine grace. We know not the corruption of our own hearts, nor what we shall do if God leaves us to ourselves. His sin was, that his heart was lifted up. What need have great men, and good men, and useful men, to study their own infirmities and follies, and their obligations to free grace, that they may never think highly of themselves; but beg earnestly of God, that he will always keep them humble! Hezekiah made a bad return to God for his favours, by making even those favours the food and fuel of his pride. Let us shun the occasions of sin: let us avoid the company, the amusements, the books, yea, the very sights that may administer to sin. Let us commit ourselves continually to God's care and protection; and beg of him never to leave us nor forsake us. Blessed be God, death will soon end the believer's conflict; then pride and every sin will be abolished. He will no more be tempted to withhold the praise which belongs to the God of his salvation.

Manasseh repents (verses 1–20)

We have already seen Manasseh's terrible wickedness.

Here Scripture records his repentance, a remarkable demonstration of God's rich forgiving mercy and renewing grace.

Manasseh lost his freedom, was separated from the advisers and companions who had encouraged evil, and faced the prospect of dying in a miserable prison.

He began to look back on his life and cry out for deliverance and mercy.

He confessed his sins, condemned himself, humbled himself before God and despised the dreadful wickedness he had committed.

Yet he still hoped to receive pardon through the Lord's abundant mercy.

Now Manasseh knew that Jehovah is God, able to save and deliver.

He learned to fear, trust, love and obey him.

From then on, his character changed and he began to walk in newness of life.

Who can tell how much pain of conscience he suffered while remembering his long years of apostasy, the many people he led into sin and destruction, and the blood of faithful people shed through his persecution?

Who can claim that the way to heaven has been closed against them when someone so wicked was admitted through repentance?

However much evil you recognize in your own heart, here is someone equally guilty who discovered the way to repent.

Do not deny yourself what God has not denied you.

It is not sin alone, but unrepentance, that keeps a sinner outside heaven.

Amon's wicked reign (verses 21–25)

Amon's father did evil, but Amon did worse.

Whatever warnings or convictions he experienced, he never humbled himself before God.

His life was soon cut short while he remained in his sins.

He stands as a warning to everyone tempted to treat God's patience and mercy toward Manasseh as permission to continue sinning.

May God help us be truthful with ourselves and judge our own character correctly before death fixes our condition forever.

Chapter Outline
Manasseh's and repentance. | (1-20) |
Amon's wicked reign in Judah. | (21-25) |
Verses 1-20
We have seen Manasseh's wickedness; here we have his repentance, and a memorable instance it is of the riches of God's pardoning mercy, and the power of his renewing grace. Deprived of his liberty, separated from his evil counsellors and companions, without any prospect but of ending his days in a wretched prison, Manasseh thought upon what had passed; he began to cry for mercy and deliverance. He confessed his sins, condemned himself, was humbled before God, loathing himself as a monster of impiety and wickedness. Yet he hoped to be pardoned through the abundant mercy of the Lord. Then Manasseh knew that Jehovah was God, able to deliver. He knew him as a God of salvation; he learned to fear, trust in, love, and obey him. From this time he bore a new character, and walked in newness of life. Who can tell what tortures of conscience, what pangs of grief, what fears of wrath, what agonizing remorse he endured, when he looked back on his many years of apostacy and rebellion against God; on his having led thousands into sin and perdition; and on his blood-guiltiness in the persecution of a number of God's children? And who can complain that the way of heaven is blocked up, when he sees such a sinner enter? Say the worst against thyself, here is one as bad who finds the way to repentance. Deny not to thyself that which God hath not denied to thee; it is not thy sin, but thy impenitence, that bars heaven against thee. ( [2Chr.33.21-2Chr.33.25] 2Ch 33:21-25)
[2Chr.33.21-2Chr.33.25]
Verses 21-25
Amon's father did ill, but he did worse. Whatever warnings or convictions he had, he never humbled himself. He was soon cut off in his sins, and made a warning for all men not to abuse the example of God's patience and mercy to Manasseh, as an encouragement to continue in sin. May God help us to be honest to ourselves, and to think aright respecting our own character, before death fixes us in an unchangeable state.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Josiah's good reign in Judah.

Josiah seeks the Lord from his youth

Our earliest childhood years cannot usually be devoted to much useful service to others.

That makes it wise to dedicate our earliest youth to God, rather than waste the short life that remains.

Happy are those who seek the Lord and prepare to be useful while young, when others are chasing sinful pleasures, acquiring destructive habits and forming harmful relationships.

Who can calculate the sorrow prevented by early faith and the blessings it produces?

Careful self-examination and vigilance reveal the deceitfulness and wickedness of our hearts and the sins within our lives.

Josiah's example encourages us to humble ourselves before God and seek him.

Believers also learn not to fear death but to welcome it when it spares them from evils still to come.

Nothing hastens a nation's ruin more than rejecting earnest attempts at reform.

God will not be mocked.

Only he can turn the deepest flow of a person's affections, raising those who are dead in trespasses and sins.

His grace in the lives of those who seek the Savior while young has a special beauty.

Has Jesus, the Day-spring from on high, visited you?

Can you, like Josiah, remember first recognizing this light and life during your youth?

What extraordinary happiness comes from knowing Jesus from one's earliest years!
classic_reading:
[2Chr.34.1]
Chapter 34
Josiah's good reign in Judah.
--As the years of infancy cannot be useful to our fellow-creatures, our earliest youth should be dedicated to God, that we may not waste any of the remaining short space of life. Happy and wise are those who seek the Lord and prepare for usefulness at an early age, when others are pursuing sinful pleasures, contracting bad habits, and forming ruinous connexions. Who can express the anguish prevented by early piety, and its blessed effects? Diligent self-examination and watchfulness will convince us of the deceitfulness and wickedness of our own hearts, and the sinfulness of our lives. We are here encouraged to humble ourselves before God, and to seek unto him, as Josiah did. And believers are here taught, not to fear death, but to welcome it, when it takes them away from the evil to come. Nothing hastens the ruin of a people, nor ripens them for it, more than their disregard of the attempts made for their reformation. Be not deceived, God is not mocked. The current and tide of affections only turns at the command of Him who raises up those that are dead in trespasses and sins. We behold peculiar loveliness, in the grace the Lord bestows on those, who in tender years seek to know and to love the Saviour. Hath Jesus, the Day-spring from on high, visited you? Can you trace your knowledge of this light and life of man, like Josiah, from your youth? Oh the unspeakable happiness of becoming acquainted with Jesus from our earliest years!

Josiah celebrates the Passover (verses 1–19)

The book of Kings describes more fully how Josiah destroyed idolatry.

Chronicles instead gives an account of his solemn celebration of the Passover.

The Lord's Supper resembles Passover more closely than any other Jewish festival.

Observing it rightly is a sign of growth in true godliness and devotion.

Only God can make our hearts holy and prepare us to worship him properly.

Nevertheless, there are duties that we must perform, through which we seek and receive his blessing.

Josiah dies in battle (verses 20–27)

Scripture does not directly condemn Josiah for confronting Pharaoh.

Yet Henry considers it possible that Josiah was wrong not to consult the Lord after receiving a warning.

His death might have corrected him for rashness.

At the same time, it was a judgment upon the hypocritical and wicked people of Judah.

For someone who has lived in repentance, faith and obedience, the unexpected or sudden manner of death cannot destroy the person's eternal hope.

The people mourned Josiah.

Yet many people grieve over disasters while refusing to abandon the sins that caused God to send them.

Only repentance can turn away divine judgment.

If we judge Josiah's conduct to have been wrong, let us also watch our own actions, lest we die in a way that dishonors our Christian confession.

The passover kept by Josiah. | (1-19) |
Josiah slain in battle. | (20-27) |
Verses 1-19
The destruction Josiah made of idolatry, was more largely related in the book of Kings. His solemnizing the passover is related here. The Lord's supper resembles the passover more than any other of the Jewish festivals; and the due observance of that ordinance, is a proof of growing piety and devotion. God alone can truly make our hearts holy, and prepare them for his holy services; but there are duties belonging to us, in doing which we obtain this blessing from the Lord.
[2Chr.35.20-2Chr.35.27]
Verses 20-27
The Scripture does not condemn Josiah's conduct in opposing Pharaoh. Yet Josiah seems to deserve blame for not inquiring of the Lord after he was warned; his death might be a rebuke for his rashness, but it was a judgment on a hypocritical and wicked people. He that lives a life of repentance, faith, and obedience, cannot be affected by the sudden manner in which he is removed. The people lamented him. Many mourn over sufferings, who will not forsake the sins that caused God to send them. Yet this alone can turn away judgments. If we blame Josiah's conduct, we should be watchful, lest we be cut down in a way dishonourable to our profession.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe destruction of Jerusalem.1–21The proclamation of Cyrus.22, 23
Jerusalem is destroyed (verses 1–21)

The ruin of Judah and Jerusalem unfolded gradually.

God repeatedly tried to call the people back through his word, ministers, conscience and the events of Providence.

These were all signs of his compassion and his desire that sinners not perish.

Consider the dreadful destruction that sin brings!

If we value our earthly blessings and want them to last, we should keep sin—the worm that attacks their root—away from them.

The people had often plowed and sown the land during seventh years when it should have rested.

Now it remained unsown and uncultivated for seventy years, ten times seven.

In the end, human disobedience cannot deprive God of the glory due to him.

If the people would not let the land rest, God would make it rest.

O Lord, what place will your justice spare if Jerusalem itself has fallen?

If the city where you delighted could be destroyed for wickedness, let us not grow proud, but fear.

Cyrus announces the return (verses 22 and 23)

God promised the restoration of the exiles and the rebuilding of Jerusalem after seventy years.

At last the appointed time to favor Zion came.

God's church may be cast down, but it is not cast off.

His people may be corrected, but they are not abandoned.

They may be put into a furnace, but they will not be destroyed or left there longer than necessary for the worthless material to be refined away.

God may contend with his people for a long time, but he will not contend forever.

As the books of Chronicles close, we should reflect on the destruction that sin has brought into the whole world—and even into God's own church.

Let us tremble at these records while recognizing in a few faithful lives that God has never left himself without witnesses.

Having considered this truthful picture of fallen human nature, compare it with human nature renewed through God's almighty grace, through the justifying righteousness of our Savior Jesus Christ that adorns the soul.

Chapter 36
Chapter Outline
The destruction of Jerusalem. | (1-21) |
The proclamation of Cyrus. | (22-23) |
Verses 1-21
The ruin of Judah and Jerusalem came on by degrees. The methods God takes to call back sinners by his word, by ministers, by conscience, by providences, are all instances of his compassion toward them, and his unwillingness that any should perish. See here what woful havoc sin makes, and, as we value the comfort and continuance of our earthly blessings, let us keep that worm from the root of them. They had many times ploughed and sowed their land in the seventh year, when it should have rested, and now it lay unploughed and unsown for ten times seven years. God will be no loser in his glory at last, by the disobedience of men. If they refused to let the land rest, God would make it rest. What place, O God, shall thy justice spare, if Jerusalem has perished? If that delight of thine were cut off for wickedness, let us not be high-minded, but fear.
[2Chr.36.22-2Chr.36.23]
Verses 22-23
God had promised the restoring of the captives, and the rebuilding of Jerusalem, at the end of seventy years; and that time to favour Zion, that set time, came at last. Though God's church be cast down, it is not cast off; though his people be corrected, they are not abandoned; though thrown into the furnace, they are not lost there, nor left there any longer than till the dross be separated. Though God contend long, he will not contend always. Before we close the books of the Chronicles, which contain a faithful register of events, think what desolation sin introduced into the world, nay, even into the church of God. Let us tremble at what is here recorded, while in the character of some few gracious souls, we discover that the Lord left not himself without witness. And when we have looked at this faithful portrait of man by nature, let us contrast with it that same nature, when recovered by Almighty grace, through the justifying and soul-adorning righteousness of Christ our Saviour.
